approachQuestion.prompt:
Combined Charges
Two nondecreasing arrays A and B define one charge A[i]+B[j] per index pair. Return the k smallest charges in nondecreasing order, preserving multiplicity of different index pairs. Example: A=[1,4], B=[2,3,8], k=4 → [3,4,6,7].

1 ≤ a=len(A), b=len(B) ≤ 100000; 1 ≤ k ≤ min(a*b,200000). Signed 32-bit values; sums fit 64 bits. Arrays are read-only. Return charges only, not index pairs. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 1 ≤ a=len(A), b=len(B) ≤ 100000; 1 ≤ k ≤ min(a*b,200000). Signed 32-bit values; sums fit 64 bits. Arrays are read-only. Return charges only, not index pairs.

options.text: Let s=min(a,k). Seed a min-heap with (A[i]+B[0],i,0) for i=0 through s−1. Repeatedly emit the minimum entry and advance only its row to j+1 if that column exists, until k charges are emitted.
options.feedback: Each row is ordered. Rows after the first k cannot contribute a strictly smaller charge than the k first-column entries already available; ties can be supplied by those earlier rows because only charge values are returned.

options.text: Enumerate every index pair, sort all sums, and return the first k.
options.feedback: This preserves multiplicity but materializes many unnecessary pairs when k is small.

options.text: Seed only pair (0,0); after removing (i,j), insert (i+1,j) and (i,j+1) without tracking visited pairs.
options.feedback: Pair (1,1) can be reached from two predecessors and counted twice. With A=[0,10], B=[0,1,100], k=5 this emits [0,1,10,11,11] instead of [0,1,10,11,100].

options.text: Return A[i]+B[i] for all common indices, sorted, taking the first k or stopping if those pairs run out.
options.feedback: The example needs off-diagonal charges 4 and 6, which this procedure omits.

feedback.reason: Each row is ordered. Rows after the first k cannot contribute a strictly smaller charge than the k first-column entries already available; ties can be supplied by those earlier rows because only charge values are returned.

Each fixed A index defines a sorted row of pair sums as B advances. Only the smallest frontier head can be next globally. Retain index pairs so duplicate charge values remain distinct requested combinations.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A with s=min(a,k), bottom-up heap construction, k emissions and a separate output list. Each heap entry has one row and column index; no visited table or full Cartesian matrix is stored. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(s + k log(s+1)) time, O(s) auxiliary space
O(ab log(ab+1)) time, O(ab) auxiliary space
O(s + k log(s+1)) time, O(k+s) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Seed s rows and perform heap work for k emitted pairs.
details: Copying s first-column entries and heapifying takes O(s). Each emitted charge causes a removal and at most one row advance, with repairs bounded by log(s+1). Interleaved rows attain that cost. Only s frontier entries are retained. The k returned values cost O(k) writing time but are excluded from auxiliary space.
“O(ab log(ab+1)) time, O(ab) auxiliary space”: This describes materializing every pair rather than generating a frontier prefix.
“O(k) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Even the s frontier entries need storage and their mutations need repair.
“O(s + k log(s+1)) time, O(k+s) auxiliary space”: The k returned charges are output, not workspace; only the frontier counts.
